{{AN chess|pos=egright}}
Lasker gave a brilliant answer on the chessboard, winning four of the first five games, and playing a type of chess Tarrasch could not understand. For example, in the second game after 19 moves arose a situation ({{em|diagram}}) in which Lasker was a [[pawn (chess)|pawn]] down, with a {{chessgloss|bad bishop}} and {{chessgloss|doubled pawns}}. At this point it appeared Tarrasch was winning, but 20 moves later he was forced to [[Rules of chess#Resigning|resign]].<ref name="Giffard398">Giffard, p.398</ref> Lasker eventually won by 10½–5½ (eight wins, five draws, and three losses). Tarrasch claimed the wet weather was the cause of his defeat.<ref name="Giffard398"/>

==== Matches against Janowski ====
{{main|World Chess Championship 1910 (Lasker–Janowski)}}

In 1909 Lasker drew a short match (two wins, two losses) against [[Dawid Janowski]], an all-out attacking [[Polish people|Polish]] expatriate. Several months later they played a longer match in Paris, and chess historians still debate whether this was for the World Chess Championship.<ref>Several authors have considered this match as a World Chess Championship, for instance:
*{{cite book
 | title=From Morphy to Fischer
 | author=Horowitz, Israel
 | publisher=Batsford
 | year=1973
 | pages=63–64
 | author-link=Israel Horowitz}}
*{{cite book
 | title=The Centenary Match – Kasparov-Karpov III
 | author=Keene, Raymond
 | author2=Goodman, David
 | publisher=Batsford
 | page=6
 | year=1986
 | isbn=0-02-028700-3
 | author-link=Raymond Keene}}
*{{cite book
 | title=Le guide des échecs
 | author=Giffard, Nicolas
 | language=fr
 | year=1993
 | publisher=[[Éditions Robert Laffont]]
 | page=400}}
More recent sources consider it was only an exhibition match:
*{{cite web
 | author=Edward Winter
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/winter38.html#5199._Lasker_v_Janowsky_Paris_1909
 | title=Chess Notes 5199
 | publisher=ChessHistory.com
 | author-link=Edward Winter (chess historian)}}
*{{cite web
 | author=Mark Weeks
 | title=1909 Lasker – Janowski Exhibition Matches
 | publisher=mark-weeks.com
 | url=http://www.mark-weeks.com/chess/09lj$wix.htm}}</ref> Understanding Janowski's style, Lasker chose to defend solidly so that Janowski unleashed his attacks too soon and left himself vulnerable. Lasker easily won the match 8–2 (seven wins, two draws, one loss).<ref name="Giffard400">{{cite book
 | title=Le guide des échecs
 | author=Giffard, Nicolas
 | language=fr
 | year=1993
 | publisher=[[Éditions Robert Laffont]]
 | page=400}}</ref> This victory was convincing for everyone but Janowski, who asked for a revenge match. Lasker accepted and they played a [[World Chess Championship 1910 (Lasker–Janowski)|World Chess Championship match]] in Berlin in November–December 1910. Lasker crushed his opponent, winning 9½–1½ (eight wins, three draws, no losses).<ref name="storiascacchiMatches1900Al1914"/> Janowski did not understand Lasker's moves, and after his first three losses he declared to [[Edward Lasker]], "Your [[homonym]] plays so stupidly that I cannot even look at the chessboard when he thinks. I am afraid I will not do anything good in this match."<ref name="Giffard400"/>

==== Match against Schlechter ====
{{main|World Chess Championship 1910 (Lasker–Schlechter)}}
[[Image:Schlechter, Carl 1896 - DPLA - 832da5245429c37f5e2ffcdf1fa3b902 (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|Schlechter would have taken Lasker's world title if he had won or drawn the last game of their 1910 match.]]
Between his two matches against Janowski, Lasker arranged another [[World Chess Championship 1910 (Lasker–Schlechter)|World Chess Championship]] in January–February 1910 against [[Carl Schlechter]]. Schlechter was a modest gentleman, who was generally unlikely to win the major chess tournaments by his peaceful inclination, his lack of aggressiveness and his willingness to accept most [[draw (chess)|draw]] [[draw by agreement|offers]] from his opponents (about 80% of his games finished by a draw).<ref name="Giffard404">Giffard 1993, p. 404</ref> 

At the beginning, Lasker tried to attack but Schlechter had no difficulty defending, so that the first four games finished in draws. In the fifth game Lasker had a big advantage, but committed a blunder that cost him the game. Hence at the middle of the match Schlechter was one point ahead. The next four games were drawn, despite fierce play from both players. In the sixth Schlechter managed to draw a game being a pawn down. In the seventh Lasker nearly lost because of a beautiful [[The exchange (chess)#The exchange sacrifice|exchange sacrifice]] from Schlechter. In the ninth only a blunder from Lasker allowed Schlechter to draw a lost [[chess endgame|ending]]. The score before the last game was thus 5–4 for Schlechter. In the tenth game Schlechter tried to win tactically and took a big advantage, but he missed a clear win at the 35th move, continued to take increasing risks and finished by losing.<ref name="Giffard406">Giffard 1993, p. 406</ref> Hence the match was a draw and Lasker remained World Champion.

It has been speculated that Schlechter played unusually risky chess in the tenth game because the terms of the match required him to win by a margin of two games.  But according to Isaak and Vladimir Linder, this was unlikely. The match was originally to be a 30-game affair and Schlechter would have to win by two games. But they note that according to the Austrian chess historian Michael Ehn, Lasker agreed to forgo the plus two provision in view of the match being subsequently reduced to only 10 games. For proof Ehn quoted Schlechter's comment printed in Allgemeine Sportzeitung (ASZ) of December 9, 1909 "There will be ten games in all. The winner on points will receive the title of world champion. If the points are equal, the decision will be made by the arbiter."
<ref>
{{cite book
| title=Emanuel Lasker, 2nd World Chess Champion
| author=Isaak and Vladimir Linder
| publisher=Russell Enterprises Inc.
| date=2010
| page=109 }}
</ref>

==== Abandoned challenges ====
In 1911 Lasker received a challenge for a world title match against the rising star [[José Raúl Capablanca]]. Lasker was unwilling to play the traditional "first to win ten games" type of match in the semi-tropical conditions of [[Havana]], especially as drawn games were becoming more frequent and the match might last for over six months. He therefore made a counter-proposal: if neither player had a lead of at least two games by the end of the match, it should be considered a draw; the match should be limited to the best of thirty games, counting draws; except that if either player won six games ''and'' led by at least two games before thirty games were completed, he should be declared the winner; the champion should decide the venue and stakes, and should have the exclusive right to publish the games; the challenger should deposit a forfeit of US$2,000 (equivalent to over $250,000 in 2020 values<ref>Using average incomes as the conversion factor; if prices are used for the conversion, the result is about $45,000—see {{cite web
 | url=http://www.measuringworth.com/uscompare/
 | title=Six Ways to Compute the Relative Value of a U.S. Dollar Amount, 1774 to Present
 | publisher=MeasuringWorth
 | access-date=June 5, 2008
}}</ref>); the time limit should be twelve moves per hour; play should be limited to two sessions of 2½ hours each per day, five days a week. Capablanca objected to the time limit, the short playing times, the thirty-game limit, and especially the requirement that he must win by two games to claim the title, which he regarded as unfair. Lasker took offence at the terms in which Capablanca criticized the two-game lead condition and broke off negotiations, and until 1914 Lasker and Capablanca were not on speaking terms. However, at the 1914 St. Petersburg tournament, Capablanca proposed a set of rules for the conduct of World Championship matches, which were accepted by all the leading players, including Lasker.<ref name="graemecree1921WorldChessChampionship">{{Cite web
 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050120165616/http://members.aol.com/graemecree/chesschamps/world/world1921.htm
 | title=1921 World Chess Championship
 | access-date=November 21, 2008
| archive-date=January 20, 2005
| url=http://members.aol.com/graemecree/chesschamps/world/world1921.htm
}} This cites: a report of Lasker's concerns about the location and duration of the match, in the ''New York Evening Post'', March 15, 1911; Capablanca's letter of December 20, 1911, to Lasker, stating his objections to Lasker's proposal; Lasker's letter to Capablanca, breaking off negotiations; Lasker's letter of April 27, 1921, to Alberto Ponce of the Havana Chess Club, proposing to resign the 1921 match; and Ponce's reply, accepting the resignation.</ref>

Late in 1912 Lasker entered into negotiations for a world title match with [[Akiba Rubinstein]], whose tournament record for the previous few years had been on a par with Lasker's and a little ahead of Capablanca's.<ref name="chessmetricsProfileRubinstein">{{cite web
 | url=http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PlayerProfile.asp?Params=188510SSSSS3S112008189006131000000000026310100
 | title=Chessmetrics Player Profile: Akiba Rubinstein
 | publisher=Chessmetrics
 | author=Jeff Sonas
 | access-date=June 4, 2008
| author-link=Jeff Sonas
 }}</ref> The two players agreed to play a match if Rubinstein could raise the funds, but Rubinstein had few rich friends to back him and the match was never played. This situation demonstrated some of the flaws inherent in the championship system then being used. The start of World War I in summer 1914 put an end to hopes that Lasker would play either Rubinstein or Capablanca for the World Championship in the near future.<ref name="Horowitz1973MorphyToFischer">{{cite book
 | title=From Morphy to Fischer
 | author=Horowitz, I.A.
 | publisher=Batsford
 | year=1973
 | author-link=Israel Horowitz
}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
 | title=Classical Chess Matches, 1907–1913
 | author=Wilson, F.
 | year=1975
 | publisher=Dover
 | isbn=0-486-23145-3
}}</ref>
Throughout World War I (1914–1918) Lasker played in only two serious chess events. He convincingly won (5½−½) a non-title match against Tarrasch in 1916.<ref name="storiascacchiMatches1915Al1929"/> In September–October 1918, shortly before the [[Armistice with Germany (Compiègne)|armistice]], he won a quadrangular (four-player) tournament, half a point ahead of Rubinstein.<ref>{{cite web
 |url         = http://www.endgame.nl/berlin1928.htm
 |title       = Berlin 1897, 1918 and 1928
 |publisher   = Endgame
 |access-date  = June 5, 2008
|url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20080619004619/http://www.endgame.nl/berlin1928.htm
 |archive-date = June 19, 2008
}}</ref>

=== Academic activities 1894–1918 ===
[[Image:Hilbert.jpg|thumb|upright|[[David Hilbert]] encouraged Lasker to obtain a [[PhD]] in mathematics.]]
Despite his superb playing results, chess was not Lasker's only interest. His parents recognized his intellectual talents, especially for mathematics, and sent the adolescent Emanuel to study in Berlin (where he found he also had a talent for chess). Lasker gained his [[abitur]] (high school graduation certificate) at [[Landsberg an der Warthe]], now a [[Poland|Polish]] town named Gorzów Wielkopolski but then part of [[Prussia]]. He then studied mathematics and philosophy at the universities in Berlin, [[Göttingen]] (where [[David Hilbert]] was one of his doctoral advisors) and [[Heidelberg]].<ref name="dcsStAndrewsLaskerBio"/>

In 1895 he published two mathematical articles in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''.<ref>{{cite journal
 | title=Metrical Relations of Plane Spaces of ''n'' Manifoldness
 | author=Lasker, Emanuel
 | journal=Nature
 | volume=52
 | issue=1345
 | pages=340–343
 |date=August 1895
 | doi=10.1038/052340d0
 |bibcode = 1895Natur..52R.340L | s2cid=4017358
 | url=https://zenodo.org/record/1429368
 }}<br />{{cite journal
 | title=About a certain Class of Curved Lines in Space of ''n'' Manifoldness
 | author=Lasker, Emanuel
 | journal=Nature
 | volume=52
 | issue=1355
 |date=October 1895
 | pages=596
 | doi=10.1038/052596a0
 |bibcode = 1895Natur..52..596L | s2cid=4016031
 | url=https://zenodo.org/record/1429372
 }}</ref> On the advice of [[David Hilbert]] he registered for doctoral studies at [[Erlangen]] during 1900–1902.<ref name="dcsStAndrewsLaskerBio"/> In 1901 he presented his doctoral thesis ''Über Reihen auf der Convergenzgrenze'' ("On Series at Convergence Boundaries") at Erlangen and in the same year it was published by the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{cite book
 | title=Great Chess Upsets
 | author=Reshevsky, Samuel
 | publisher=Arco
 | year=1976
 | isbn=0-668-03492-0
 | author-link=Samuel Reshevsky
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
 | journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A
 | title=Über Reihen auf der Convergenzgrenze
 | author=Lasker, Emanuel
 | year=1901
 | volume=196
 | issue=274–286
 | pages=431–477
 | bibcode=1901RSPTA.196..431L
 | doi=10.1098/rsta.1901.0009
| doi-access=
 }}</ref> He was awarded a doctorate in mathematics in 1902.<ref name="dcsStAndrewsLaskerBio"/> His most significant mathematical article, published in 1905, established a [[Lasker–Noether theorem|theorem on primary decompositions]] of which [[Emmy Noether]] developed a more generalized form, which is now regarded as of fundamental importance to [[abstract algebra]] and [[algebraic geometry]].<ref>{{Cite journal
 |first   = E.
 |last    = Lasker
 |title   = Zur Theorie der Moduln und Ideale
 |journal = Math. Ann.
 |volume  = 60
 |year    = 1905
 |issue   = 1
 |pages   = 20–116
 |doi     = 10.1007/BF01447495
 |s2cid = 120367750
 |url     = https://eudml.org/doc/158174 }}<br />{{Cite journal
 |author1-link = Emmy Noether
 |title        = Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen
 |year         = 1921
 |journal      = [[Mathematische Annalen]]
 |volume       = 83
 |issue        = 1
 |doi          = 10.1007/BF01464225
 |author       = Noether, Emmy
 |pages        = 24–66
 |url          = http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/index.php?id=11&PPN=PPN235181684_0083&DMDID=DMDLOG_0008&L=1
 |bibcode      = 1921MatAn..83...24N
 |s2cid = 121594471
 |access-date  = September 30, 2013
|archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20160305071858/http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/index.php?id=11&PPN=PPN235181684_0083&DMDID=DMDLOG_0008&L=1
 |archive-date = March 5, 2016
|url-status     = dead
}} For the relationship between Lasker's work and Noether's see {{cite encyclopedia
 |url        = https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Lasker_ring
 |title      = Lasker ring
 |encyclopedia       = [[Encyclopedia of Mathematics]]
 |publisher  = Springer
 |access-date = May 31, 2008
}}</ref><ref name="dcsStAndrewsLaskerBio"/>

Lasker held short-term positions as a mathematics lecturer at [[Tulane University]] in [[New Orleans, Louisiana|New Orleans]] (1893) and [[Victoria University of Manchester|Victoria University]] in [[Manchester]] (1901; Victoria University was one of the "parents" of the current [[University of Manchester]]).<ref name="dcsStAndrewsLaskerBio"/> However, he was unable to secure a longer-term position, and pursued his scholarly interests independently.<ref name="laskergesellschaftLaskerNewApproaches">{{cite web
 |url          = http://www.lasker-gesellschaft.de/forum/johannes-fischer/lasker-new-approaches.html
 |title        = Lasker: New Approaches
 |publisher    = Lasker-Gesellschaft
 |access-date   = November 21, 2008
|archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20110726190525/http://www.lasker-gesellschaft.de/forum/johannes-fischer/lasker-new-approaches.html
 |archive-date = July 26, 2011
|url-status     = dead
}}; also available at {{cite web
 |url        = http://www.chesscafe.com/text/skittles158.pdf
 |title      = Lasker: New Approaches
 |publisher  = ChessCafe
 |access-date = May 2, 2008
}}. This refers to {{cite book
 | title=Emanuel Lasker: Schach, Philosophie und Wissenschaft (Emanuel Lasker: Chess, Philosophy and Science)
 | author=Sieg, Ulrich
 | author2=Dreyer, Michael
 | publisher=Philo
 | year=2001
 | isbn=3-8257-0216-2
}}.</ref>

In 1906 Lasker published a booklet titled ''Kampf'' (''Struggle''),<ref name="Lasker1906Kampf">Many sources say ''Kampf'' was published in 1907, but Lasker said 1906 - {{cite book |author=Lasker |first=Emanuel |url=https://archive.org/details/laskersmanualofc0000unse_y2w5/mode/2up |title=Lasker's Manual of Chess |date=1960 |publisher=Dover |isbn= |orig-year=1932 |url-access=registration}}</ref> in which he attempted to create a general theory of all competitive activities, including chess, business and war. He produced two other books which are generally categorized as philosophy, ''Das Begreifen der Welt'' (''Comprehending the World''; 1913) and ''Die Philosophie des Unvollendbar'' (sic; ''The Philosophy of the Unattainable''; 1918).<ref name="dcsStAndrewsLaskerBio"/>

=== Other activities 1894–1918 ===
In 1896–97 Lasker published his book ''Common Sense in Chess'', based on lectures he had given in London in 1895.<ref>{{cite book |author=Lasker, Emanuel |url=https://archive.org/details/commonsenseinche0000lask |title=Common Sense in Chess |date=1965 |publisher=Dover |isbn=0-486-21440-0 |orig-year=1896 (German edition) |url-access=registration}}</ref>

{{Chess diagram small
| floatright
| [[Rice Gambit]]

|rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|__|__|rd
|pd|pd|pd|__|__|pd|__|pd
|__|__|__|bd|__|nd|__|__
|__|__|__|pl|nl|__|__|__
|__|__|bl|__|__|pd|pd|pl
|__|__|__|__|__|__|__|__
|pl|pl|pl|pl|__|__|pl|__
|rl|nl|bl|ql|__|rl|kl|__
| {{hidden|multiline=y|ta1=left|fw1=normal| Position after 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5 Nf6 6.Bc4 d5 7.exd5 Bd6 8.0-0 | White [[sacrifice (chess)|sacrifices]] the knight on e5 in order to get his king to safety and enable a rook to join the attack against the under-developed black position.}}
}}
{{algebraic notation|pos=egright}}

In 1903, Lasker played in [[Ostend]] against [[Mikhail Chigorin]], a six-game match that was sponsored by the wealthy lawyer and industrialist [[Isaac Rice (businessman)|Isaac Rice]] in order to test the [[Rice Gambit]].<ref>{{cite journal
 | journal=New York Times
 | title=Chess World's Doings; Lasker to Test Rice Gambit
 | date=August 2, 1903
| url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1903/08/02/101312061.pdf
 | access-date=May 2, 2008
}}</ref> Lasker narrowly lost the match. Three years later Lasker became secretary of the Rice Gambit Association, founded by Rice in order to promote the Rice Gambit,<ref name="BillWallEmLasker"/> and in 1907 Lasker quoted with approval Rice's views on the convergence of chess and military strategy.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | pages=35
 | journal=Lasker's Chess Magazine
 | date=November 1907
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/winter29.html
 | title=Chess Notes by Edward Winter
 | access-date=May 2, 2008
}}</ref>

In November 1904, Lasker founded ''Lasker's Chess Magazine'', which ran until 1909.<ref>{{cite web
 |url        = http://moravian-chess.cz/katalog.php?idkat=11
 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070704013603/http://www.moravian-chess.cz/katalog.php?idkat=11
 |url-status   = dead
 |archive-date = July 4, 2007
|title      = Moravian chess publishing – Catalogue
 |publisher  = Moravian Chess
 |access-date = May 2, 2008
}}</ref>

Beginning in 1910, he wrote a weekly chess column for the [[New York Evening Post]], for which he was Chess Editor.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Emanuel Lasker |url=https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/lasker-emanuel |encyclopedia=[[Jewish Virtual Library]] |access-date=April 11, 2021}}</ref>

Emanuel Lasker became interested in the strategy game [[Go (board game)|Go]] after being introduced to it by his namesake [[Edward Lasker]], probably in 1907 or 1908 (Edward Lasker wrote a successful book ''Go and Go-Moku'' in 1934<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/rec.games.go/LGH6DOZtaZc|title=Google Groups|website=groups.google.com|access-date=April 7, 2016}}</ref>). He and Edward played Go together while Edward was helping him prepare for his 1908 match with Tarrasch. He kept his interest in Go for the rest of his life, becoming one of the strongest players in Germany and Europe and contributing occasionally to the magazine ''Deutsche Go-Zeitung''. It is alleged that he once said "Had I discovered Go sooner, I would probably have never become world chess champion".<ref>Forster, Richard; Negele, Michael; Tischbierek, Raj (eds.): ''Emanuel Lasker: volume II, choices and chances, chess and other games of the mind'' – Berlin, Excelsior Verlag, 2020, {{ISBN|978-3-935800-10-5}}, Chapter 4, pages 165–213: ''Lasker and Go'', Theo van Ees and Hans-Christian Wolfarth.</ref>

At the age of 42, in July 1911, Lasker married Martha Cohn (née Bamberger), a rich widow who was a year older than Lasker and already a grandmother. They lived in Berlin.<ref name="BillWallEmLasker"/><ref>{{cite book
 | title=Emanuel Lasker: The Life of a Chess Master
 | author=Hannak, J.
 | publisher=Simon & Schuster
 | year=1959
 | pages=152, 160–61
}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
 | author=Hooper, D.
 | author2=Whyld, K.
 | title=The Oxford Companion to Chess
 | edition=2
 | year=1992
 | page=[https://archive.org/details/oxfordcompaniont0000hoop/page/218 218]
 | isbn=0-19-866164-9
| title-link=The Oxford Companion to Chess
 | publisher=Oxford University Press
 }}</ref> Martha Cohn wrote popular stories under the pseudonym "L. Marco".<ref name="laskergesellschaftLaskerNewApproaches"/><ref>{{cite book
 | title=Emanuel Lasker: The Life of a Chess Master
 | author=Hannak, J.
 | publisher=Simon & Schuster
 | year=1959
 | page=125
}}</ref>

During [[World War I]], Lasker invested all of his savings in German [[war bond]]s, which lost nearly their entire value with the wartime and [[hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic|post-war inflation]]. During the war, he wrote a pamphlet which claimed that civilization would be in danger if Germany lost the war.<ref name="BillWallEmLasker"/>

=== Match against Capablanca ===
{{main|World Chess Championship 1921|}}
In January 1920 Lasker and [[José Raúl Capablanca]] signed an agreement to play a World Championship match in 1921, noting that Capablanca was not free to play in 1920. Because of the delay, Lasker insisted on a final clause that allowed him to play anyone else for the championship in 1920, that nullified the contract with Capablanca if Lasker lost a title match in 1920, and that stipulated that if Lasker resigned the title Capablanca should become World Champion. Lasker had previously included in his agreement before World War I to play [[Akiba Rubinstein]] for the title a similar clause that if he resigned the title, it should become Rubinstein's.<ref name="WinterHowCapaBecameChampion"/>

A report in the ''American Chess Bulletin'' (July–August 1920 issue) said that Lasker had resigned the world title in favor of Capablanca because the conditions of the match were unpopular in the chess world. The ''American Chess Bulletin'' speculated that the conditions were not sufficiently unpopular to warrant resignation of the title, and that Lasker's real concern was that there was not enough financial backing to justify his devoting nine months to the match.<ref name="WinterHowCapaBecameChampion">{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/capablanca2.html
 | title=How Capablanca Became World Champion
 | author=Winter, Edward
 | publisher=ChessHistory
 | access-date=June 5, 2008
| author-link=Edward Winter (chess historian)
}} Winter cites: ''American Chess Bulletin'' (July–August 1920 issue) for Lasker's resignation of the title, the ''ACB''{{'s}} theory about Lasker's real motive and Havana's offer of $20,000; [[Amos Burn]] in ''The Field'' of July 3, 1920, the ''British Chess Magazine'' of August 1920 and other sources for protestations that Lasker had no right to nominate a successor; [[Amos Burn]] in ''The Field'' of July 3, 1920, and E.S. Tinsley in ''The Times'' (London) of June 26, 1920, for criticism of the conditions Lasker set for the defense of the title; ''American Chess Bulletin'' September–October 1920 for Lasker's and Capablanca's statements that Capablanca was the champion and Lasker the challenger, for Capablanca's statement that Lasker's contract with Rubinstein had contained a clause allowing him to abdicate in favor of Rubinstein, for Lasker's intention to resign the title if he beat Capablanca and his support for an international organization, preferably based in the Americas, to manage international chess. Winter says that before Lasker's abdication some chess correspondents had been calling for Lasker to be stripped of the title. For a very detailed account given by Capablanca after the match, see {{Cite journal
 | journal=British Chess Magazine
 | author=Capablanca, José Raúl
 | date=October 1922
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/capablancalasker.html
 | title=Capablanca's Reply to Lasker (presented by Edward Winter)
 | access-date=June 5, 2008
| author-link=José Raúl Capablanca
}}</ref> When Lasker resigned the title in favor of Capablanca he was unaware that enthusiasts in [[Havana]] had just raised $20,000 to fund the match provided it was played there. When Capablanca learned of Lasker's resignation he went to the Netherlands, where Lasker was living at the time, to inform him that Havana would finance the match. In August 1920 Lasker agreed to play in Havana, but insisted that he was the challenger as Capablanca was now the champion. Capablanca signed an agreement that accepted this point, and soon afterwards published a letter confirming this. Lasker also stated that, if he beat Capablanca, he would resign the title so that younger masters could compete for it.<ref name="WinterHowCapaBecameChampion"/>

The match was played in March–April 1921. After four draws, the fifth game saw Lasker [[blunder (chess)|blunder]] with Black in an equal [[chess endgame|ending]]. Capablanca's solid style allowed him to easily draw the next four games, without taking any risks. In the tenth game, Lasker as White played a position with an [[Isolated Queen Pawn]] but failed to create the necessary activity and Capablanca reached a superior ending, which he duly won. The eleventh and fourteenth games were also won by Capablanca, and Lasker resigned the match.<ref>{{cite book
 | title=Le guide des échecs
 | author=Giffard, Nicolas
 | language=fr
 | year=1993
 | publisher=[[Éditions Robert Laffont]]
 | page=412
}}</ref>

[[Reuben Fine]] and [[Harry Golombek]] attributed this to Lasker's being in mysteriously poor form.<ref name="Fine1952WorldsGreatChessGamesEmLasker"/><ref>{{cite book |author= |title=Capablanca's Hundred Best Games of Chess |publisher=G. Bell & Sons |year=1959 |isbn= |editor=Golombek |editor-first=Harry |page=59 |chapter=On the Way to the World Championship}}</ref> On the other hand, [[Vladimir Kramnik]] thought that Lasker played quite well and the match was an "even and fascinating fight" until Lasker blundered in the last game, and explained that Capablanca was 20 years younger, a slightly stronger player, and had more recent competitive practice.<ref name="KramnikSteinitzToKasparov"/> In a post mortem of the match, Lasker said the Habanero weather severely impaired his chess ability, and his physical health declined.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lasker |first=Emanuel |date=1922|publisher=Walter de Gruyter GmbH |title=Mein Wettkampf mit Capablanca|isbn= ((9783112684993))<!-- isbn goes to reprint by same publisher --> }} As quoted in {{cite web|url=https://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/laskerhavana.html|title=Lasker on the 1921 World Championship Match|first=Edward|last=Winter|work=Chess Notes|access-date=2026-05-07}}</ref> Capablance challenged his assertion, proclaiming "two or three days after the match was over, Dr. Lasker sailed for Europe looking very well and cheerful, far, very far, from the sick man one would imagine after reading his book."<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Capablanca|first=José Raúl|title=My Reply to Dr. Lasker|magazine=[[British Chess Magazine]]|access-date=April 29, 2026|url=https://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/capablancalasker.html|date=1922|location=Leeds|volume=42}}</ref>

=== European life and travels ===
Lasker was in his early 50s when he lost the world championship to Capablanca, and he retired from serious match play afterwards;<ref name="storiascacchiMatches1915Al1929"/><ref name="storiascacchiMatches1930Al1949">{{cite web
 | url=http://xoomer.virgilio.it/cserica/scacchi/storiascacchi/matches/1930-49.htm
 | title=I matches 1930/49
 | publisher=La grande storia degli scacchi
 | access-date=September 3, 2009
}}</ref> his only other match was a short exhibition against [[Frank James Marshall]] in 1940, which was never completed due to Lasker's illness, and death a few months later.<ref name="Hannak" />{{rp|311}} After winning the [[Moravská Ostrava 1923 chess tournament]] (without a single loss) and the [[New York 1924 chess tournament]] (1½ points ahead of Capablanca) and finishing second at Moscow in 1925 (1½ points behind [[Efim Bogoljubow]], ½ point ahead of Capablanca),<ref name="storiascacchiTornei1920Al1929"/> he effectively retired from serious chess.<ref name="Fine1952WorldsGreatChessGamesEmLasker"/>

[[Image:Lasker.png|thumb|Emanuel Lasker (left) and his elder brother [[Berthold Lasker|Berthold]] in 1907]]
During the [[Moscow 1925 chess tournament]], Lasker received a telegram informing him that the drama written by himself and his brother [[Berthold Lasker|Berthold]], ''{{ill|Vom Menschen die Geschichte|de}}'' ("History of Mankind"), had been accepted for performance at the Lessing theatre in Berlin. Lasker was so distracted by this news that he lost badly to [[Carlos Torre]] the same day.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessbase.com/newsdetail.asp?newsid=3779
 | title=Production of Lasker trainer cancelled
 | date=April 7, 2007
| publisher=ChessBase
 | access-date=May 2, 2008
}} includes an image of part of the original newspaper report.</ref> The play, however, was not a success.<ref name="laskergesellschaftLaskerNewApproaches"/>

In 1926, Lasker wrote ''Lehrbuch des Schachspiels'', which he re-wrote in English in 1927 as ''[[Lasker's Manual of Chess]]''.<ref name="LaskersManualOfChess">{{cite book |author=Lasker |first=Emanuel |url=https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.525138/page/5/mode/2up |title=Lasker's Manual of Chess |date=1960 |publisher=Dover |isbn= |orig-year= |url-access=registration}}</ref> He also wrote books on other games of mental skill: ''Encyclopedia of Games'' (1929) and ''Das verständige Kartenspiel'' (means "Sensible Card Play"; 1929; English translation in the same year), both of which posed a problem in the [[Mathematical game|mathematical analysis of card games]];<ref name="Wastlund2005TwoPersonSingleSuitWhist">{{cite journal
 | title=A solution of two-person single-suit whist
 | author=Johan Wăstlund
 | journal=The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics
 | volume=12
 | date=September 5, 2005
| url=http://www.emis.de/journals/EJC/Volume_12/PDF/v12i1r43.pdf
 | access-date=June 6, 2008
}}</ref> ''Brettspiele der Völker'' ("Board Games of the Nations"; 1931), which includes 30 pages about [[Go (board game)|Go]] and a section about a game he had invented in 1911, [[Lasca]].<ref name="ResearchInterfaceLasca">{{cite web
 |url         = http://research.interface.co.uk/lasca/about.htm
 |title       = About Lasca – a little-known abstract game
 |access-date  = June 6, 2008
|publisher   = Human–Computer Interface Research
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20080509062029/http://research.interface.co.uk/lasca/about.htm
 |archive-date = May 9, 2008
}}</ref>

In 1930, Lasker was a special correspondent for Dutch and German newspapers<ref name="Culbertson">{{cite book | last = Culbertson | first = Ely | author-link = Ely Culbertson | title = The Strange Lives of One Man | publisher = The John C. Winston Company | pages = 552–553| location = Chicago | year= 1940 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/culbertson.html}}</ref> reporting on the [[Ely Culbertson#Anglo-American matches|Culbertson-Buller]] bridge match during which he became a registered teacher of the [[Ely Culbertson|Culbertson]] system.<ref name=Culbertson/> He became an expert bridge player,<ref name="Laskeratbridge">A detailed examination of Emanuel Lasker's involvement in bridge is provided by the chapter ''Nicht nur Schach Emanuel Lasker als Bridgespieler'' by Robert van de Velde on pages 332–363 of ''Emanuel Lasker Denker Weltenbürger Schachweltmeister'' edited by Richard Forster, Stefan Hansen and Michael Negele (Berlin, 2009).</ref> representing Germany at international events in the early 1930s,<ref name="BillWallEmLasker"/><ref name="Giffard394"/> and wrote ''Das Bridgespiel'' ("The Game of [[Contract bridge|Bridge]]") in 1931.<ref name="WinterBridge">{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/bridge.html
 | title=Chess and Bridge
 | publisher=ChessHistory
 | access-date=June 6, 2008
}}</ref>

In October 1928 Emanuel Lasker's brother [[Berthold Lasker|Berthold]] died.<ref name="BillWallEmLasker"/><ref>{{cite book |author=Hannak |first=J. |url=https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.525138/page/5/mode/2up |title=Emanuel Lasker: The Life of a Chess Master |publisher=Andre Deutsch |year=1952 |isbn= |page=266 |url-access=registration}}</ref>

In spring 1933 [[Adolf Hitler]] started a campaign of [[Nazi boycott of Jewish businesses|discrimination and intimidation]] against [[Jew]]s, depriving them of their property and citizenship. Lasker and his wife Martha, who were both Jewish, were forced to leave Germany in the same year.<ref>{{cite book |author=Hannak |first=J. |url=https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.525138/page/5/mode/2up |title=Emanuel Lasker: The Life of a Chess Master |publisher=Andre Deutsch |year=1951 |isbn= |page=268 |url-access=registration}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
 | author=Hooper, D.
 | author2=Whyld, K.
 | title=The Oxford Companion to Chess
 | url=https://archive.org/details/oxfordcompaniont0000hoop
 | url-access=registration
 | edition=2
 | year=1992
 | page=[https://archive.org/details/oxfordcompaniont0000hoop/page/218 218]
 | publisher=Oxford University Press
 | isbn=0-19-866164-9
}}</ref> After a short stay in England, in 1935 they were invited to live in the USSR by [[Nikolai Krylenko]], the Soviet Sports Minister and an enthusiastic supporter of chess.<ref name="laskergesellschaftLaskerNewApproaches"/> In the USSR, Lasker renounced his German citizenship and received Soviet citizenship.<ref>{{cite book
 |author1=Litmanowicz, Władysław  |author2=Giżycki, Jerzy
 | title=Szachy od A do Z
 | publisher=Wydawnictwo Sport i Turystyka Warszawa
 | year=1986
 | isbn=83-217-2481-7 
 | id=(1. A-M), (2. N-Z)
}}</ref> He took permanent residence in Moscow, and was given a post at Moscow's Institute for Mathematics<ref name="laskergesellschaftLaskerNewApproaches"/> and a post of trainer of the USSR national team.<ref>{{cite book
 | author=Weinstein, Boris Samoilovich
 | title='''Myslitel''' (''Thinker'')
 | publisher=Fizkultura i sport
 | year=1981
 | pages=104 (Russian edition)
 }}</ref>
Lasker returned to competitive chess to make some money, finishing fifth in [[Zürich 1934 chess tournament|Zürich 1934]] and third in [[Moscow 1935 chess tournament|Moscow 1935]] (undefeated, ½ point behind [[Mikhail Botvinnik]] and [[Salo Flohr]]; ahead of Capablanca, [[Rudolf Spielmann]] and several Soviet masters), sixth in Moscow 1936 and equal seventh in [[Nottingham 1936 chess tournament|Nottingham 1936]].<ref name="storiascacchiTornei1930Al1939"/> His performance in Moscow 1935 at age 66 was hailed as "a biological miracle".<ref>{{cite book
 | author=Reuben Fine
 | title=The World's Great Chess Games
 | publisher=Dover
 | year=1976
 | page=51
 | isbn=0-486-24512-8
}}</ref>

===Settling in the United States===
In August 1937, Martha and Emanuel Lasker decided to leave the Soviet Union, and they moved, via the Netherlands, to the United States (first Chicago, next New York) in October 1937.<ref>{{cite book
 | author=Weinstein, Boris Samoilovich
 | title='''Myslitel''' (''Thinker'')
 | publisher=Fizkultura i sport
 | year=1981
 | pages=105 (Russian edition)
 }}</ref> They were visiting Martha's daughter, but they may also have been motivated by political upheaval in the Soviet Union.<ref>{{cite book
| title=Emanuel Lasker, 2nd World Chess Champion
| author=Isaak and Vladimir Linder
| publisher=Russell Enterprises Inc.
| date=2010
| page=244 }}
</ref> In the United States Lasker tried to support himself by giving chess and bridge lectures and exhibitions, as he was now too old for serious competition.<ref name="BillWallEmLasker"/><ref name="laskergesellschaftLaskerNewApproaches"/> In 1940 he published his last book, ''The Community of the Future'', in which he proposed solutions for serious political problems, including [[anti-Semitism]] and unemployment.<ref name="laskergesellschaftLaskerNewApproaches"/>

== Assessment ==
=== Playing strength and style ===
Lasker was considered to have a "psychological" method of play in which he considered the subjective qualities of his opponent, in addition to the objective requirements of his position on the board. [[Richard Réti]] published a lengthy analysis of Lasker's play in which he concluded that Lasker deliberately played inferior moves that he knew would make his opponent uncomfortable.<ref>Réti wrote, "In analyzing Lasker's tournament games, I was struck by his lasting and at first seemingly incredible good luck. ... There is no denying the fact that over and over again Lasker's exposition is poor, that he is in a losing position hundreds of times and, nevertheless, wins in the end."{{cite book
 | author=Réti, Richard
 | title=Masters of the Chessboard
 | publisher=Dover Publications
 | year=1976
 | page=132
 | isbn=0-486-23384-7
}} Réti considered, but rejected as too improbable, the "hypothesis of lasting luck", finally concluding that the only explanation for Lasker's repeated success from bad positions is that he "often plays badly on purpose". ''Id.'' Réti concluded that Lasker studied his opponents' strong and weak points, and that, "He is not so much interested in making the objectively best moves as he is in making those most disagreeable to his opponent; he turns the game in a direction not suitable to the style of his opponent and on this unaccustomed road leads him to the abyss, often by means of intentionally bad moves, as I have previously described." ''Id.'' at 133.</ref> [[William Pollock (chess player)|W. H. K. Pollock]] commented, "It is no easy matter to reply correctly to Lasker's bad moves."<ref>{{cite book |author=Rowland |first=Mrs. F. F. |url=https://archive.org/details/pollockmemories00pollgoog |title=Pollock Memories: A Collection of Chess Games, Problems, &c., &c. |publisher=Chess Player's Chronicle |year=1899 |isbn= |page=78}}</ref>

Lasker himself denied the claim that he deliberately played bad moves, and most modern writers agree. According to [[Grandmaster (chess)|Grandmaster]] [[Andrew Soltis]] and [[International Master]] [[John L. Watson]], the features that made his play mysterious to contemporaries now appear regularly in modern play: [[Sacrifice (chess)|sacrifices]] to gain positional advantage; playing the "practical" move rather than trying to find the best move; counterattacking and complicating the game before a disadvantage became serious.<ref name="SoltisLaskerMatters">{{cite book
 | title=Why Lasker Matters
 | author=Soltis, A.
 | publisher=Batsford
 | year=2005
 | page=5
 | isbn=0-7134-8983-9
 | url=http://www.chesscenter.com/twic/jwatsonbkrev80.html
 | access-date=July 24, 2007
| archive-date=January 4, 2009
| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090104125727/http://www.chesscenter.com/twic/jwatsonbkrev80.html
 | url-status=dead
 }} The URL is a review by [[John L. Watson]]. Another review, with examples, is at {{cite web
 | url=http://www.chesscafe.com/text/review538.pdf
 | access-date=January 1, 2009
| title=Analyzing an Enigma
 | publisher=ChessCafe
 | author=Taylor Kingston
 }}</ref><ref>"Lasker's greatest skill in defense was his ability to render a normal (inferior) position chaotic": {{cite book
 | author=Crouch, C.
 | title=How to Defend in Chess
 | publisher=Everyman
 | year=2000
 | isbn=1-85744-250-4
}}; review including this quotation at {{cite web
 | title=How to Defend in Chess: review
 | author=Watson, J.
 | url=http://www.jeremysilman.com/book_reviews_jw/jw_ht_defend_chess.html
 | publisher=JeremySilman
 | access-date=November 19, 2008
| archive-date=September 7, 2008
| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080907232517/http://www.jeremysilman.com/book_reviews_jw/jw_ht_defend_chess.html
 | url-status=dead
 }}</ref> Former World Champion [[Vladimir Kramnik]] said, "He realized that different types of advantage could be interchangeable: tactical edge could be converted into strategic advantage and vice versa", which mystified contemporaries who were just becoming used to the theories of Steinitz as codified by [[Siegbert Tarrasch]].<ref name="KramnikSteinitzToKasparov"/>

[[Max Euwe]] opined that the real reason behind Lasker's success was his "exceptional defensive technique" and that "almost all there is to say about defensive chess can be demonstrated by examples from the games of Steinitz and Lasker", the former exemplifying passive defence and the latter an active defence.<ref>{{cite book
 | author=[[Max Euwe]] and Hans Kramer
 | title=The Middlegame
 | publisher=Hays Publishing
 | year=1994
 | pages=93, 101
}}</ref>

The famous win against [[José Raúl Capablanca]] at [[St. Petersburg 1914 chess tournament|St. Petersburg in 1914]], which Lasker needed in order to retain any chance of catching up with Capablanca, is sometimes offered as evidence of his "psychological" approach. [[Reuben Fine]] describes Lasker's choice of opening, the [[Ruy Lopez, Exchange Variation|Exchange Variation of the Ruy Lopez]], as "innocuous but psychologically potent".<ref name="Fine1952WorldsGreatChessGamesEmLasker"/> [[Luděk Pachman]] writes that Lasker's choice presented his opponent with a [[dilemma]]: with only a ½&nbsp;point lead, Capablanca would have wanted to play safe; but the Exchange Variation's [[pawn structure]] gives White an [[Chess endgame|endgame]] advantage, and Black must use his {{chessgloss|bishop pair}} aggressively in the [[middlegame]] to nullify this.<ref name="Pachman1987StPetersburg1914">{{cite book|last=Pachman|first=L.|title=Decisive Games in Chess History|publisher=Courier Dover|year=1987|pages=64–68|chapter=St&nbsp;Petersburg 1914: Drawing Variation – The Way to Victory|isbn=0-486-25323-6|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jlgJTCyonAgC&q=capablanca&pg=PA1|access-date=June 4, 2009}}</ref> However, an analysis of Lasker's use of this variation throughout his career concludes that he had excellent results with it as White against top-class opponents, and sometimes used it in "must-win" situations.<ref name="WrinnLaskerRuyExchangeVariation">As White in [[Ruy Lopez, Exchange Variation|Exchange Variation of the Ruy Lopez]] Lasker scored ten wins, three draws and just one loss, to Steinitz in 1894. Lasker also won the three recorded games in which he played the variation as Black; one was against [[Alexander Alekhine|Alekhine]], in the 1914 St. Petersburg Tournament, the day before Lasker beat Capablanca.{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chesscafe.com/text/skittles230.pdf
 | title=Lasker and the Exchange Variation of the Ruy Lopez – Part 1
 | author=Wrinn, Steve
 | access-date=June 9, 2008
| publisher=ChessCafe
 }} and {{cite web
 | url=http://www.chesscafe.com/text/skittles232.pdf
 | title=Lasker and the Exchange Variation of the Ruy Lopez – Part 2
 | author=Wrinn, Steve
 | access-date=June 9, 2008
| publisher=ChessCafe
 }}</ref> In Kramnik's opinion, Lasker's play in this game demonstrated deep positional understanding, rather than psychology.<ref name="KramnikSteinitzToKasparov">{{cite web
 |url          = http://www.kramnik.com/eng/interviews/getinterview.aspx?id=61
 |access-date   = January 2, 2009
|title        = Kramnik Interview: From Steinitz to Kasparov
 |author       = Vladimir Kramnik
 |publisher    = Kramnik.com
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20080512052013/http://www.kramnik.com/eng/interviews/getinterview.aspx?id=61
 |archive-date = May 12, 2008
|url-status     = dead
|author-link = Vladimir Kramnik
 }}</ref>

Fine reckoned Lasker paid little attention to the openings,<ref name="Fine1952WorldsGreatChessGamesEmLasker"/> while Capablanca thought that Lasker knew the openings very well but disagreed with a lot of contemporary opening analysis. Before the 1894 world title match, Lasker studied the openings thoroughly, especially Steinitz's favorite lines. In Capablanca's opinion, no player surpassed Lasker in the ability to assess a position quickly and accurately, in terms of who had the better prospects of winning and what strategy each side should adopt.<ref name="HavanurReviewWhyLaskerMatters">{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessville.com/reviews/WhyLaskerMatters2.htm
 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071124073054/http://chessville.com/reviews/WhyLaskerMatters2.htm
 | url-status=usurped
 | archive-date=November 24, 2007
| title=Why Lasker Matters – review by Nagesh Havanur
 | author=Nagesh Havanur
 | publisher=ChessVille
 | access-date=November 21, 2008
}}</ref> Capablanca also wrote that Lasker was so adaptable that he played in no definite style, and that he was both a tenacious defender and a very efficient finisher of his own attacks.<ref>{{Cite news
 | author=Capablanca, José Raúl
 | title=The Ideal Style of the Masters
 | newspaper=Mundial
 | date=May 1927
 | pages=1–4
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/capablanca3.html
 | access-date=January 2, 2009
| author-link=José Raúl Capablanca
}}</ref>

Lasker followed [[Wilhelm Steinitz|Steinitz]]'s principles, and both demonstrated a completely different chess paradigm than the "romantic" mentality before them. Thanks to Steinitz and Lasker, positional players gradually became common ([[Siegbert Tarrasch|Tarrasch]], [[Carl Schlechter|Schlechter]], and [[Akiba Rubinstein|Rubinstein]] stand out.) But, while Steinitz created a new school of chess thought, Lasker's talents were far harder for the masses to grasp; hence there was no Lasker school.<ref>{{cite book
 | author=Garry Kasparov
 | title=My Great Predecessors – Part I
 | publisher=Everyman Chess
 | year=2003
 | pages=187–222
 | isbn=1857443306
}}</ref>

In addition to his enormous chess skill, Lasker was said to have an excellent competitive temperament: his rival [[Siegbert Tarrasch]] once said, "Lasker occasionally loses a game, but he never loses his head."<ref name="Fine1952WorldsGreatChessGamesEmLasker"/> Lasker enjoyed the need to adapt to varying styles and to the shifting fortunes of tournaments.<ref name="UXLEncyclopediaBiography"/> Although very strong in matches, he was even stronger in tournaments. For over 20 years, he always finished ahead of the younger Capablanca: at St. Petersburg 1914, New York 1924, Moscow 1925, and Moscow 1935.<ref>{{cite book
 | author=Harry Golombek
 | title=Capablanca's 100 Best Games of Chess
 | publisher=David McKay
 | year=1978
 | pages=37, 88, 116, 222
 | isbn=0-679-14044-1
}}</ref> Only in 1936 (15 years after their match), when Lasker was 67, did Capablanca finish ahead of him.<ref>{{cite book
 | author=Reuben Fine
 | title=The World's Great Chess Games
 | publisher=Dover
 | year=1976
 | page=50
 | isbn=0-486-24512-8
}}</ref>

In 1964, ''Chessworld'' magazine published an article in which future World Champion [[Bobby Fischer]] listed the ten greatest players in history.<ref>Bobby Fischer, "The Ten Greatest Masters in History", ''Chessworld'', Vol. 1, No. 1 (January–February 1964), pp. 56–61.</ref> Fischer did not include Lasker in the list, deriding him as a "coffee-house player [who] knew nothing about openings and didn't understand positional chess".<ref>Fischer, "The Ten Greatest Masters in History", p. 59.</ref> In a poll of the world's leading players taken some time after Fischer's list appeared, Tal, Korchnoi, and [[Robert Byrne (chess player)|Robert Byrne]] all said that Lasker was the greatest player ever.<ref>{{cite book
 | title=Profile of a Prodigy
 | author=Brady, Frank
 | publisher=David McKay
 | year=1973
 | edition=2nd
 | page=78
 | isbn=0-486-25925-0
}}</ref> Both [[Pal Benko]] and Byrne stated that Fischer later reconsidered and said that Lasker was a great player.<ref name="Benko">{{cite book
 | title=Pal Benko: My Life, Games and Compositions
 | author1=Benko, Pal
 | author2=Silman, Jeremy
 | publisher=Siles Press
 | year=2003
 | page=429
 | isbn=1-890085-08-1
}}</ref><ref>Brady 1973, p. 79.</ref>

Statistical ranking systems place Lasker high among the greatest players of all time. The book ''Warriors of the Mind'' places him sixth, behind [[Garry Kasparov]], [[Anatoly Karpov]], Fischer, [[Mikhail Botvinnik]] and Capablanca.<ref name="WarriorsOfTheMind">{{Cite book
 | title=Warriors of the Mind
 | last1=Keene
 | first1=Raymond
 | author1-link=Raymond Keene
 | last2=Divinsky
 | first2=Nathan
 | author2-link=Nathan Divinsky
 | year=1989
 | publisher=Hardinge Simpole
 | location=Brighton, UK
 | isbn=0-9513757-2-5
}} See the summary list at {{cite web
 |url=http://chess.eusa.ed.ac.uk/Chess/Trivia/AlltimeList.html 
 |access-date=November 21, 2008 |publisher=Edinburgh University Chess Club 
 |title=All Time Rankings 
 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091126000035/http://chess.eusa.ed.ac.uk/Chess/Trivia/AlltimeList.html 
 |archive-date=November 26, 2009 }}</ref> In his 1978 book ''The Rating of Chessplayers, Past and Present'', [[Arpad Elo]] gave retrospective ratings to players based on their performance over the best five-year span of their career. He concluded that Lasker was the joint second strongest player of those surveyed (tied with Botvinnik and behind Capablanca).<ref>{{cite book
 | title=The Rating of Chessplayers, Past and Present
 | author=Elo, A.
 | year=1978
 | publisher=Arco
 | isbn=0-668-04721-6
 | url=http://www.chessbase.com/newsdetail.asp?newsid=1160
 | author-link=Arpad Elo
}} The URL provides greater detail, covering 47&nbsp;players whom Elo rated, and notes that [[Bobby Fischer]] and [[Anatoly Karpov]] would have topped the list if the January 1, 1978, [[FIDE]] ratings had been included (FIDE ratings use Elo's system).</ref> The most up-to-date system, [[Chessmetrics]], is rather sensitive to the length of the periods being compared, and ranks Lasker between fifth and second strongest of all time for peak periods ranging in length from one to twenty years.<ref>{{cite web
 |url=http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSS1S000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |title=Peak Average Ratings: 1 year peak range 
 |publisher=Chessmetrics 
 |author=Jeff Sonas 
 |access-date=June 10, 2008 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309155451/http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSS1S000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |archive-date=March 9, 2012 |author-link=Jeff Sonas 
 }}{{cite web
 |url=http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSS5S000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |title=Peak Average Ratings: 5 year peak range 
 |publisher=Chessmetrics 
 |author=Jeff Sonas 
 |access-date=June 10, 2008 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309154749/http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSS5S000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |archive-date=March 9, 2012 |author-link=Jeff Sonas 
 }}{{cite web
 |url=http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSSTS000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |title=Peak Average Ratings: 10 year peak range 
 |publisher=Chessmetrics 
 |author=Jeff Sonas 
 |access-date=June 10, 2008 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309155152/http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSSTS000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |archive-date=March 9, 2012 |author-link=Jeff Sonas 
 }}{{cite web
 |url=http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSSFS000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |title=Peak Average Ratings: 15 year peak range 
 |publisher=Chessmetrics 
 |author=Jeff Sonas 
 |access-date=June 10, 2008 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309154756/http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSSFS000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |archive-date=March 9, 2012 |author-link=Jeff Sonas 
 }}{{cite web
 |url=http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSSWS000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |title=Peak Average Ratings: 20 year peak range 
 |publisher=Chessmetrics 
 |author=Jeff Sonas 
 |access-date=June 10, 2008 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309155602/http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PeakList.asp?Params=199510SSSSSWS000000000000111000000000000010100 
 |archive-date=March 9, 2012 |author-link=Jeff Sonas 
 }}</ref> Its author, the statistician [[Jeff Sonas]], concluded that only Kasparov and Karpov surpassed Lasker's long-term dominance of the game.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessbase.com/newsdetail.asp?newsid=2409
 | title=The Greatest Chess Player of All Time – Part IV
 | author=Jeff Sonas
 | publisher=ChessBase
 | year=2005
 | access-date=November 19, 2008
| author-link=Jeff Sonas
 }} Part IV gives links to all three earlier parts.</ref> By Chessmetrics' reckoning, Lasker was the number 1 player in 292 different months—a total of over 24 years. His first No. 1 rank was in June 1890, and his last in December 1926—a span of 36½ years.<ref>{{cite web
| title=Chessmetrics Player Profile: Emanuel Lasker | publisher=Chessmetrics.com
| url=http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/PlayerProfile.asp?Params=199510SSSSS3S073076000000111000000000017510100
| access-date=June 5, 2009
}}</ref> Chessmetrics also considers him the strongest 67-year-old in history: in December 1935, at age 67 years and 0 months, his rating was 2691 (number 7 in the world), well above second-place [[Viktor Korchnoi]]'s rating at that age (2660, number 39 in the world, in March 1998).<ref>{{cite web
| title=Age-Aligned Rating List: 67 years, 0 months | publisher=Chessmetrics.com
| url=http://chessmetrics.com/cm/CM2/SingleAge.asp?Params=188510SSSSS3S073076193512131000000000000010804
| access-date=November 11, 2009
}}</ref>

=== Influence on chess ===
[[Image:Bundesarchiv Bild 102-14194, Emanuel Lasker.jpg|thumb|upright|Lasker at home in Berlin, in 1933]]
Lasker founded no school of players who played in a similar style.<ref name="Fine1952WorldsGreatChessGamesEmLasker"/> [[Max Euwe]], World Champion 1935–1937 and a prolific writer of chess manuals, who had a lifetime 0–3 score against Lasker,<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chess.pl?yearcomp=exactly&year=&playercomp=either&pid=&player=Euwe&pid2=&player2=Lasker&movescomp=exactly&moves=&opening=&eco=&result=
 | title=Euwe–Lasker Results
 | author=ChessGames.com
 | access-date=December 3, 2008
}}</ref> said, "It is not possible to learn much from him. One can only stand and wonder."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Soltis |first=Andrew |date=October 19, 2019 |title=Britannica: The Evolution of Chess Theory (Part 2) |url=https://en.chessbase.com/post/britannica-the-development-of-chess-theory-2 |website=Chessbase}}</ref>  Lasker's pragmatic, combative approach had a great influence on [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] players like [[Mikhail Tal]] and [[Viktor Korchnoi]].<ref name="CrouchOnLasker">{{cite book
 | author=Crouch, C.
 | year=2000
 | title=How to Defend in Chess
 | publisher=Everyman Chess
 | page=115
 | isbn=1-85744-250-4
}}</ref>

There are several "Lasker Variations" in the [[chess opening]]s, including Lasker's Defense to the [[Queen's Gambit]], Lasker's Defense to the [[Evans Gambit]] (which effectively ended the use of this [[gambit]] in tournament play until a revival in the 1990s),<ref name="FineIdeasBehindOpenings">Lasker's Defense: {{cite book |author=Fine |first=Reuben |url=https://archive.org/details/ideasbehindchess0000reub |title=The Ideas Behind the Chess Openings |publisher=McKay |year=1973 |isbn= |page=63 |url-access=registration}} </ref><ref>{{cite book |author=De Firmian |first=Nick |title=Batsford's Modern Chess Openings |publisher=Batsford |year=2000 |isbn= |page=26 |chapter=Evans Gambit}}</ref> and the Lasker Variation in the McCutcheon Variation of the [[French Defense]].<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessville.com/instruction/Openings/French_Defense/instr_open_french_eco.htm
 | archive-url=https://archive.today/20130102051639/http://www.chessville.com/instruction/Openings/French_Defense/instr_open_french_eco.htm
 | url-status=usurped
 | archive-date=January 2, 2013
| title=French Defense
 | publisher=ChessVille.com
 | access-date=June 10, 2008
}}</ref>

Lasker was shocked by the poverty in which [[Wilhelm Steinitz]] died and did not intend to die in similar circumstances.<ref>Lasker wrote: "I who vanquished him must see to it that his great achievement, his theories should find justice, and I must avenge the wrongs he suffered". {{cite book |author=Lasker |first=Emanuel |url=https://archive.org/details/laskersmanualofc0000unse_y2w5 |title=Lasker's Manual of Chess |date=1960 |publisher=Dover |isbn= |access-date= |orig-year=1925}}</ref> He became notorious for demanding high fees for playing matches and tournaments, and he argued that players should own the [[copyright]] to their games rather than let publishers get all the profits.<ref name="UXLEncyclopediaBiography"/><ref name="wikisourceLaskersChessMagazineVol1">{{cite journal
 | journal=[[Lasker's Chess Magazine]]
 | volume=1
 | date=January 1905
 | url=http://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Lasker%27s_Chess_Magazine/Volume_1
 | title=From the Editorial Chair
 | author=Lasker, Emanuel
 | access-date=May 31, 2008
}}</ref> These demands initially angered editors and other players, but helped to pave the way for the rise of full-time chess professionals who earn most of their living from playing, writing and teaching.<ref name="UXLEncyclopediaBiography"/> Copyright in chess games had been contentious at least as far back as the mid-1840s,<ref name="WinterChessNote4767">{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/winter29.html#4767._Copyright
 | title=Chess Note 4767 Copyright
 | publisher=ChessHistory.com
 | author=Edward Winter
 | access-date=June 25, 2008
}}</ref> and Steinitz and Lasker vigorously asserted that players should own the copyright and wrote copyright clauses into their match contracts.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/copyright.html
 | title=Copyright on Chess Games
 | publisher=ChessHistory.com
 | author=Edward Winter
 | access-date=January 11, 2022
}}</ref> However, Lasker's demands that challengers should raise large purses prevented or delayed some eagerly awaited World Championship matches—for example [[Frank James Marshall]] challenged him in 1904 to a match for the World Championship but could not raise the stakes demanded by Lasker until 1907.<ref name="Horowitz1973MorphyToFischer"/><ref name="dcsStAndrewsLaskerBio">{{cite web
 | url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Lasker/
 | title=Lasker biography
 | publisher=University of St Andrews
 | access-date=May 31, 2008
}}</ref> This problem continued throughout the reign of his successor, Capablanca.<ref name="chessmaniacCapablancaOnlineTribute">{{cite web
 | title=Jose Raul Capablanca: Online Chess Tribute
 | url=http://www.chessmaniac.com/2007/06/jose-raul-capablanca-online-chess.php
 | date=June 28, 2007
| publisher=ChessManiac.com
 | access-date=May 20, 2008
| archive-date=May 13, 2008
| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080513151615/http://www.chessmaniac.com/2007/06/jose-raul-capablanca-online-chess.php
 | url-status=dead
 }}</ref><ref name="chessgamesNewYork1924">{{cite web
 | title=New York 1924
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chesscollection?cid=1007158
 | publisher=ChessGames.com
 | access-date=May 20, 2008
}}</ref>

Some of the controversial conditions that Lasker insisted on for championship matches led Capablanca to attempt twice (1914 and 1922) to publish rules for such matches, to which other top players readily agreed.<ref name="graemecree1921WorldChessChampionship"/><ref name="chessvilleLondonRules">{{cite web
 |url         = http://www.chessville.com/misc/History/Mad_Aussie_Trivia_Archive_Three.htm
 |title       = The Mad Aussie's Chess Trivia – Archive #3
 |author      = Graham Clayton
 |publisher   = ChessVille.com
 |access-date  = June 9, 2008
|url-status     = usurped
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20080516220224/http://www.chessville.com/misc/History/Mad_Aussie_Trivia_Archive_Three.htm
 |archive-date = May 16, 2008
}}</ref>

=== Work in other fields ===
In a 1905 article on [[commutative algebra]], Lasker introduced the theory of [[Lasker–Noether theorem|primary decomposition]] of [[ideal of a ring|ideal]]s, which has influence in the theory of [[Noetherian ring]]s.<ref>He defined the [[primary decomposition]] property of the [[ring ideal|ideal]]s of some [[commutative ring]]s when he proved that [[polynomial ring]]s have the primary decomposition property.</ref> Primary decomposition rings are called "Laskerian rings" in his honor.<ref name="dcsStAndrewsLaskerBio"/><ref>{{cite book
 | title=Unknown Quantity: A Real and Imaginary History of Algebra
 | author=Derbyshire, J.
 | publisher=National Academy Press
 | date=December 2006
 | isbn=0-309-09657-X
 | chapter=12: The Lady of the Rings
 | pages=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780309096577/page/234 234–235]
 | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5SIPdYbUhU0C&q=lasker+einstein+hannak&pg=PP1
 | access-date=December 29, 2008
| url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780309096577/page/234
 }}</ref>

His attempt to create a general theory of all competitive activities were followed by more consistent efforts from [[John von Neumann|von Neumann]] on [[game theory]],<ref name="LeonardCreationOfGameTheory">{{cite web
 | url=http://www.cesmep.unito.it/WP/2007/7_WP_Cesmep.pdf
 | title=Working Paper – New Light on von Neumann: politics, psychology and the creation of game theory
 | author=Leonard, J.
 | publisher=Department of Economics, University of Turin
 | access-date=May 1, 2008
| archive-date=June 26, 2008
| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080626194932/http://www.cesmep.unito.it/WP/2007/7_WP_Cesmep.pdf
 | url-status=dead
 }}</ref> and his later writings about card games presented a significant issue in the [[Mathematical game|mathematical analysis of card games]].<ref name="Wastlund2005TwoPersonSingleSuitWhist"/>
According to mathematician R. J. Nowakowski, he "came close to a complete theory of [[impartial game]]s."<ref>Richard J. Nowakowski, ''Preface'' in: Richard J. Nowakowski, Bruce M. Landman, Florian Luca, Melvyn B. Nathanson,
Jaroslav Nešetřil, and Aaron Robertson (Eds.)
''Combinatorial Game Theory'', De Gruyter Proceedings in
Mathematics, 2022.</ref>

However, his dramatic and philosophical works have never been highly regarded.<ref name="laskergesellschaftLaskerNewApproaches"/>

==Death==
Lasker died of a [[kidney]] infection in New York on January 11, 1941, at the age of 72, as a charity patient at the [[Mount Sinai Hospital (Manhattan)|Mount Sinai Hospital]]. His funeral service was held at the [[Riverside Memorial Chapel]],<ref>{{Cite news|date=January 14, 1941|title=LEADERS IN CHESS AT LASKER SERVICE; 200 Attend Rites for the Former Champion of the World (Published 1941)|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1941/01/14/archives/leaders-in-chess-at-lasker-service-200-attend-rites-for-the-former.html|access-date=January 9, 2021|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and he was buried at historic [[Beth Olam Cemetery]], Queens, New York.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Steinitz|first=William|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NltT4BinugsC&pg=PA265|title=The Steinitz Papers: Letters and Documents of the First World Chess Champion|date=August 27, 2002|publisher=McFarland|isbn=978-0-7864-1193-1|location=|pages=265|language=en}}</ref><ref>[https://en.chessbase.com/post/visiting-steinitz-and-lasker-at-their-final-resting-places ChessBase: Visiting Steinitz and Lasker at Their Final Resting Places]</ref>

== Personal life, family and friends==
His wife Martha and his sister, Mrs. Lotta Hirschberg, survived him.<ref>{{cite web
 | title=5076. Lasker's last words
 | author=Winter, Edward
 | url=http://www.chesshistory.com/winter/winter36.html#5076._Laskers_last_words_C.N._4705
 | publisher=ChessHistory
 | access-date=December 28, 2008
}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
 | author=Landsberger, K.
 | title=The Steinitz Papers: Letters and Documents of the First World Chess Champion
 | publisher=McFarland
 | year=2002
 | isbn= 0-7864-1193-7
 | page=295
 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NltT4BinugsC&q=lasker+capablanca+1921&pg=PA295
 | access-date=December 28, 2008
}}</ref>

Poet [[Else Lasker-Schüler]] was his sister-in-law.

[[Edward Lasker]], born in Kempen (Kępno), [[Greater Poland]] (then [[Prussia]]), the German-American [[International Master|chess master]], engineer, and author, claimed that he was distantly related to Emanuel Lasker.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://billwall.phpwebhosting.com/articles/relatives.htm |access-date=April 19, 2023 |title=Relatives of Chess Masters |website=Bill Wall's Chess Paage |author=Bill Wall }}</ref> They both played in the great [[New York 1924 chess tournament]].<ref>{{cite magazine
 | last=Lasker
 | first=Edward
 | date=March 1974
 | title=The New York Tournament of 1924
 | magazine=Chess Life & Review
 | quote=I did not discover that we were actually related until he told me shortly before his death that someone had shown him a Lasker family tree on one of whose branches I was dangling
}}</ref>

Lasker was a good friend of [[Albert Einstein]], who wrote the introduction to the posthumous biography, ''Emanuel Lasker: The Life of a Chess Master,'' by Jacques Hannak (1952).<ref>{{cite book |author=Hannak |first=J. |url=https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.525138/page/5/mode/2up |title=Emanuel Lasker: The Life of a Chess Master |publisher=Andre Deutsch |year=1951 |isbn= |access-date=}}</ref> In the preface Einstein expressed satisfaction for having met Lasker:
{{blockquote|Emanuel Lasker was undoubtedly one of the most interesting people I came to know in my later years. We must be thankful to those who have penned the story of his life for this and succeeding generations. For there are few men who have had a warm interest in all the great human problems and at the same time kept their personality so uniquely independent.}}

==In popular culture==
In [[Michael Chabon]]'s [[alternate history]] [[Mystery fiction|mystery]] novel, ''[[The Yiddish Policemen's Union]]'', the murdered man, Mendel Shpilman (born during the 1960s), being a chess enthusiast, uses the name "Emanuel Lasker" as an alias. The reference is clearly understood by the protagonist, Detective Meyer Landsman, because he has also studied chess.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rafferty |first=Terrence |date=May 13, 2007 |title=Cops and Rabbis (Published 2007) |language=en |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/05/13/books/review/Rafferty-t.html |access-date=July 29, 2023}}</ref>

== Notable games ==
*Lasker vs. Johann Hermann Bauer, Amsterdam 1889.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1026352
 | title=Emanuel Lasker vs. Johann Hermann Bauer, Amsterdam 1889
 | website=[[Chessgames.com]]
}}</ref> Although this was not the earliest-known game with a successful two-bishops [[sacrifice (chess)|sacrifice]], this combination is now known as a "Lasker–Bauer combination" or "Lasker sacrifice".<ref name="JeffreysReviewWhyLaskerMatters">{{cite web |author=Michael Jeffreys |title=Why Lasker Matters – review by Michael Jeffreys |url=http://www.chessville.com/reviews/WhyLaskerMatters.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061025133133/http://www.chessville.com/reviews/WhyLaskerMatters.htm |url-status=usurped |archive-date=October 25, 2006 |access-date=June 10, 2008 |publisher=ChessVille.com}}</ref>
*Harry Nelson Pillsbury vs. Lasker, St&nbsp;Petersburg 1895.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1109097
 | title=Harry Nelson Pillsbury vs. Emanuel Lasker, St&nbsp;Petersburg 1895
 | website=[[Chessgames.com]]
}}</ref> A brilliant sacrifice on the 17th move leads to a victorious attack.<ref name="Fine1952WorldsGreatChessGamesEmLasker" />
*Wilhelm Steinitz vs. Lasker, London 1899.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1132758
 | title=Wilhelm Steinitz vs. Emanuel Lasker, London 1899
 | website=[[Chessgames.com]]
}}</ref> The old champion and the new one really go for it.<ref>{{cite book
| title=500 Master Games of Chess |author1=Tartakower, S.G.  |author2=du Mont, J. | publisher=Courier Dover Publications | year=1975 | isbn=0-486-23208-5 | page=[https://archive.org/details/500mastergamesof00tart/page/270 270] (game number 209)
| url=https://archive.org/details/500mastergamesof00tart | url-access=registration | quote=steinitz lasker. | access-date=December 29, 2008
}}</ref>
*Frank James Marshall vs. Lasker, World Championship Match 1907, game 1.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1094674
 | title=Frank James Marshall vs. Emanuel Lasker, World Championship Match 1907, game 1
 | website=[[Chessgames.com]]
}}</ref> Lasker's attack is insufficient for a quick win, so he trades it in for an [[chess endgame|endgame]] in which he quickly ties Marshall in knots.<ref>{{cite book
| title=Chess Fundamentals | author=Capablanca, J.R. | chapter=Example 30 | isbn=1-85744-073-0 | edition=Algebraic, 1994
| chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/chessfundamental00capa/chessfundamental00capa_djvu.txt | access-date=December 29, 2008
| year=1994
| publisher=Everyman Chess
| location=London
}} A key position is discussed at {{cite web
| url=https://chessforallages.blogspot.com/2006/12/endgame-marshall-lasker-1907-match-game.html | access-date=December 29, 2008
| title=Endgame: Marshall – Lasker, 1907 Match, Game 1 | author=Mark Weeks
}}</ref>
*Lasker vs. Carl Schlechter, match 1910, game 10.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1121156
 | title=Emanuel Lasker vs. Carl Schlechter, match 1910, game 10
 | website=[[Chessgames.com]]
}}</ref> Not a great game, but the one that saved Lasker from losing his world title in 1910.<ref name="Pachman1987DecisiveGamesWCh1910">{{cite book
| title=Decisive Games in Chess History | author=Pachman, L.
| publisher=Courier Dover Publications | year=1987 | isbn=0-486-25323-6
| pages=48–51 | chapter=11: World Championship Match 1910
| chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jlgJTCyonAgC&q=lasker+schlechter+1910&pg=PA48 | access-date=December 29, 2008 | others=Russell, A.S.
}}</ref>
*Lasker vs. Jose Raul Capablanca, St&nbsp;Petersburg 1914.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1258181
 | title=Emanuel Lasker vs. Jose Raul Capablanca, St&nbsp;Petersburg 1914
 | website=[[Chessgames.com]]
}}</ref> Lasker, who needed a win here, surprisingly used a {{chessgloss|quiet}} opening, allowing Capablanca to {{chessgloss|simplify}} the game early. There has been much debate about whether Lasker's approach represented subtle psychology or deep positional understanding.<ref name="Fine1952WorldsGreatChessGamesEmLasker" /><ref name="KramnikSteinitzToKasparov" /><ref name="Pachman1987StPetersburg1914" />
*Max Euwe vs. Lasker, Zurich 1934.<ref>{{cite web
 | url=http://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1008008
 | title=Max Euwe vs. Emanuel Lasker, Zurich 1934
 | website=[[Chessgames.com]]
}}</ref> 66-year-old Lasker beats a future World Champion, sacrificing his queen to turn defence into attack.<ref>{{cite book | title=How to Defend in Chess: Learn from the World Champions | author=Crouch, C. | publisher=Gambit Publications | year=2007 | isbn=978-1-904600-83-1 | chapter=Game 9 | chapter-url=http://www.jeremysilman.com/book_reviews_jw/jw_ht_defend_chess.html | access-date=December 29, 2008 | archive-date=September 7, 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080907232517/http://www.jeremysilman.com/book_reviews_jw/jw_ht_defend_chess.html | url-status=dead }}</ref>
